items.title: Kaiser Permanente nurses say AI surveillance and call time tracking worsen jobs and patient care amid contract talks [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Kaiser Permanente nurses who handle advice and triage calls report that workplace surveillance, including AI monitoring of call length, empathy, and tone, is pressuring them and harming patient care. Nurses say spending more than 15 minutes on a call often leads to criticism or performance reviews, despite the complexity of some cases. The California Nurses Association is negotiating a new contract with Kaiser, where AI use is a key issue, following previous strikes and protests against AI monitoring. Kaiser Permanente defends its AI use as prioritizing patient safety with human oversight and denies using average call time to assess performance. Nurses describe situations where they felt forced to limit compassionate care to avoid negative evaluations. The company is California's largest private employer, and its AI practices could influence broader healthcare industry standards. California lawmakers are also considering bills to regulate AI in healthcare workplaces, including protections for clinicians who override automated recommendations.

items.title: StateofOpenSource.ai reports open source AI models lead adoption with 79% developer use but face operational challenges in production deployment [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: StateofOpenSource.ai highlights the growing adoption of open source AI models, with 79% of developers integrating them compared to 71% for closed models, though only 51% of open model teams reach production versus 63% for closed models. The report showcases diverse global projects using open AI, from language models for indigenous languages in New Zealand to medical and agricultural applications in Africa, emphasizing open source as a commercial market with significant enterprise use and multiple revenue models. The analysis notes that while open weights have reached parity in many capabilities, operational tooling and trust remain challenges for open source AI deployment. It also discusses the strategic importance of AI sovereignty for nations, the evolving role of agentic harnesses above AI models, and the competitive landscape where open source continues to grow alongside closed models, particularly in commodity workloads rather than frontier AI capabilities.

items.title: Moonshot AI launches Kimi K3, a 2.8 trillion parameter model priced at $3/$15 per million tokens, outperforming some competitors and promising open weights by July 2026 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Chinese AI lab Moonshot AI announced Kimi K3, their most capable model to date with 2.8 trillion parameters, available via their website and API with an open weight release planned by July 27, 2026. The model claims to outperform several competitors like Claude Opus 4.8 max and GPT-5.5 high, while trailing behind Claude Fable 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol, and is the leading model on Arena.ai's Frontend Code arena. Kimi K3 is priced at $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, making it the most expensive model released by a Chinese AI lab so far. It shows improvements in token efficiency and cost per task compared to previous versions. The author tested the model using a benchmark prompt to generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle, highlighting its reasoning token usage, cost, and vision capabilities. While the pelican benchmark is no longer a reliable measure of overall model quality, it remains useful for initial testing and understanding model characteristics.

items.title: Individual tests AI detection evasion using Claude Code and multiple agents but fails to bypass Pangram's AI detection on AI-generated text [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: An individual conducted an experiment to evade AI detection on a corpus heavily written by AI using Claude Code and 10 parallel agents, applying various editing strategies informed by a Wikipedia article on AI writing detection. Despite iterative attempts and access to the Pangram API to assess AI detection scores, nearly all posts were still flagged as 100% AI-generated. The experiment included rounds of minor edits, iterative API-guided rewrites, and attempts to mimic the writing style of a known human author to evade detection. A control test confirmed the detector accurately labeled human-authored blogs as human. The results suggest current AI detection tools remain effective against AI-generated content even when AI is used to attempt evasion.

items.title: Ask HN: User requests access to Claude AI model code for general users [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A user posted on Hacker News seeking information about the availability of the Claude AI model's code for ordinary users. The inquiry focuses on whether the AI model's code can be accessed or used by the general public.

items.title: Flathub bans low-quality AI-generated app submissions after data shows 73% abandonment rate among rejected projects [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Flathub implemented a ban on AI-generated app submissions labeled as low quality or "AI slop" following concerns about maintenance and review workload. Analysis of 120 rejected AI-heavy projects revealed that nearly three-quarters were abandoned within months, supporting the platform's decision to maintain content quality. The data, gathered by Linux developer Evangelos Paterakis, showed that 88 of the rejected repositories were no longer actively developed, with many deleting their source code. This high abandonment rate suggests that the banned AI-coded apps were unlikely to be sustained or improved, alleviating fears that the ban would push users to other platforms. Flathub volunteers manually tag submissions with the "AI Slop 1" label when signs indicate heavy AI use without human oversight, such as automated manifests or chatbot-driven communication. The ban aims to prevent volunteer reviewers from being overwhelmed by low-effort submissions and encourages developers to use AI tools responsibly alongside human skill and maintenance commitment.

items.title: Researchers propose a three-level hierarchical learning architecture for autonomous UAV swarms in search and rescue, integrating neuroplasticity, multi-agent reinforcement learning, and meta-learning with formal safety and performance guarantees [ ~ ] [ ⬢ ]
items.content_text: A new hierarchical learning architecture has been developed for autonomous UAV swarms conducting search and rescue missions, combining three distinct learning mechanisms that correspond to biological reflexes, skills, and reasoning. The system uses Hebbian neuroplasticity for individual adaptation, multi-agent reinforcement learning with graph neural networks and behavior trees for tactical coordination, and model-agnostic meta-learning with BDI reasoning and a digital twin for strategic decision-making, all formalized through architectural contracts ensuring safety, optimality, and consistency. The framework introduces Swarm Meta Cognition, allowing the swarm to monitor and adapt its cognitive strategies dynamically. Theoretical analysis shows that this hybrid neuro-symbolic system addresses key limitations of existing hierarchical reinforcement learning methods and provides guarantees such as cognitive resilience and graceful degradation in dynamic environments.

items.title: HG-RAG introduces hierarchy-guided retrieval for language models using structured knowledge graphs to improve multi-hop and relational reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: HG-RAG (Hierarchy-Guided Retrieval-Augmented Generation) is a new framework that enhances retrieval for language models by performing graph traversal over hierarchical knowledge graphs instead of flat document stores. It expands context through parent, neighbor, and child nodes based on query anchors to provide structured information. Evaluations across different graph sizes and query types show that HG-RAG outperforms dense retrieval baselines on hierarchical, relational, and multi-hop reasoning tasks. The approach also reduces hallucinations and maintains context coherence, addressing limitations of traditional retrieval-augmented generation systems in handling structured knowledge.

items.title: IMEX introduces interaction-based model explanation using Static and Interaction Correlation Power metrics to identify key features and interactions in predictive models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: IMEX (Interaction-Based Model Explanation) is a new approach in explainable predictive modeling that identifies important variables and their interactions influencing model predictions without limiting interaction order. It uses two metrics: Static Correlation Power (PCS) to measure individual feature contributions and Interaction Correlation Power (PCI) to capture complex feature interactions, enabling a detailed interpretability map of model decisions. The method was experimentally validated against INVASE on synthetic datasets with known structures, demonstrating its ability to recover relevant feature-level patterns even in the presence of non-linear, conditional, and multicollinear relationships. IMEX aims to enhance transparency and understanding of black-box predictive models by revealing latent mechanisms behind predictions.

items.title: RegNetAgents launches AI multi-agent framework for cross-network regulatory driver identification in cancer genomics, integrating TCGA and GREmLN data for breast and colorectal cancer analysis [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: RegNetAgents is an AI-based multi-agent framework designed to identify regulatory candidate genes across heterogeneous gene regulatory networks in cancer genomics. It integrates bulk tumor data from TCGA with single-cell regulatory networks from the GREmLN project to analyze breast and colorectal cancer genes, performing classification, cancer gene filtering, and mode-of-action assignment to rank candidates by evidence consistency across networks. The system operates as a downstream analytical layer over precomputed networks and is accessible via a Python API. Its application showed significant enrichment of known cancer genes among identified candidates, with no enrichment in control gene sets, indicating specificity. Additional modules evaluate oncogenic potential, druggability, clinical relevance, and network vulnerability, supporting comprehensive biological interpretation from candidate identification to hypothesis generation.

items.title: Researchers introduce Dialogue Place Recognition, a conversational visual place recognition method using interactive reasoning and natural language to improve localization accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers have developed Dialogue Place Recognition (DlgPR), a new approach that treats visual place recognition as an interactive dialogue-driven reasoning process to address ambiguity and incomplete natural language descriptions. They created DlgQuest-Cities, a large-scale dialogue-based benchmark dataset, and DQ-pilot, an intelligent questioner trained via supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning to guide the reasoning process. Experimental results show that this framework outperforms existing baseline methods, and the code and models have been made publicly available.

items.title: Researchers develop LLM-T1D, an interpretable insulin pump controller combining reinforcement learning and large language models for Type 1 Diabetes management [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers have created LLM-T1D, an insulin pump controller that integrates reinforcement learning with large language models to improve transparency and trust in Type 1 Diabetes management. The system explains its insulin delivery decisions in clear language, aiming to overcome the black-box nature of previous AI approaches. Tested on an FDA-approved simulator, LLM-T1D demonstrated improved blood sugar control with 73.5% time in range while maintaining safety against erroneous outputs.

items.title: Researchers propose a six-step framework using Large Language Models to construct Bayesian Belief Networks for decision support, demonstrated by modeling healthcare consultation intentions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A new methodology combines expert judgment and data-driven learning by using Large Language Models as AI agents to estimate probabilities for Bayesian Belief Networks (BBNs). This approach applies a trimmed-mean rule to reduce noise and was illustrated by modeling customer intention to consult a doctor in an alternative healthcare system, revealing that subjective norms have a stronger causal impact than self-efficacy. The findings suggest that improving both confidence and community norms is the most effective strategy for influencing customer decisions.

items.title: Researchers propose Capability Convergence Hypothesis showing hybrid sequence model architectures, not scale alone, determine capability limits under fixed inference budgets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A recent study introduces the Capability Convergence Hypothesis (CCH), which argues that while model representations converge with scale, capability convergence depends on architectural access structures rather than scale alone. The research identifies three fundamental resource limitations-termed the Shannon wall, horizon wall, and circuit wall-that restrict model capabilities and demonstrates that hybrid architectures combining compressive constant-state and scalable verbatim-index channels can overcome these limits. The study supports its claims through theoretical analysis and pre-registered experiments, including tests on a witness task called the Newton's-apple problem. It distinguishes proven information-theoretic lower bounds from conjectured trends in model convergence, emphasizing that capability improvements require specific hybrid access structures rather than mere scaling of model size or depth.

items.title: Researchers introduce ToolAnchor to improve large language model agents' adaptation to new tools by injecting counterfactual contexts and agentic post-training [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers have developed ToolAnchor, a framework designed to enhance large language model agents' ability to incorporate new tools without retraining from scratch by addressing behavioral inertia through counterfactual anchor contexts. The method uses teacher models to generate these contexts, verifies them with student rollouts, and internalizes successful strategies via agentic post-training. Evaluations on tasks including AI assistance, textual search, and visual search demonstrate that ToolAnchor improves agent performance when expanding toolsets, offering a scalable approach for dynamic tool adaptation in AI agents.

items.title: Researchers enhance reasoning in small language models using knowledge graph grounding and neuro-symbolic agentic framework with RGCN hints [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers propose a neuro-symbolic agentic framework to improve reasoning in small language models (SLMs) like Gemma 3 and Llama 3.2 by grounding them in knowledge graphs using symbolic triplet extraction and expert hints from a Relational Graph Convolutional Network (RGCN). They evaluate this approach on the CLUTRR kinship benchmark under both Oracle and Realistic scenarios, showing a 1.5 to 2 times performance improvement over baselines when using RGCN hints. The study identifies key challenges including an extraction bottleneck and sequential deductive fragility, where early errors compound in multi-hop reasoning. It also finds a "distraction effect" in some architectures where noisy self-generated facts reduce performance despite expert hints. The work outlines the difficulties of symbolic grounding in low-resource agentic systems and suggests iterative verification as a path forward for neuro-symbolic pipelines.

items.title: Researchers introduce pypowsybl-mcp, an MCP-based interface enabling multi-agent AI to conduct power grid simulations and analyses with human oversight [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: This position paper explores the use of Agentic AI and Model Context Protocol (MCP) to enhance power-grid studies within Transmission System Operator (TSO) environments. It focuses on integrating Large Language Models with numerical simulation tools, structured workflows, and human supervision to meet industrial requirements for agent-assisted grid studies. The authors present pypowsybl-mcp, an MCP-based interface that allows AI agents to set up simulations, execute analyses, retrieve results, and interact with power-system simulators through standardized tool calls, providing a testbed for multi-agent workflows. The paper also discusses principles for human-in-the-loop multi-agent workflows and proposes an evaluation strategy combining technical metrics with practitioner feedback. This work positions MCP-based tool integration as a foundational step toward creating more interactive, auditable, and scalable environments for power grid studies.

items.title: Researchers introduce MemoHarness, an adaptive agent harness framework that learns from execution experience to optimize control layers for large language model agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: MemoHarness is a new framework designed to improve agent harnesses, which are external control layers that manage context, tools, and outputs for large language model (LLM) agents. Unlike traditional fixed harnesses, MemoHarness learns from its own executions by decomposing the harness into six control dimensions and storing experience in a dual-layer bank, enabling adaptation to new cases without additional labels or search. Evaluations on benchmarks including shell-agent tasks, code generation, and analytical reasoning show that MemoHarness outperforms fixed harnesses and can selectively transfer learning to unseen test suites and base models. The framework also maintains cost efficiency by caching retrieved experience, suggesting that execution experience is a practical basis for building more adaptive agent harnesses, though further work is needed to assess statistical robustness and component attribution.

items.title: Researchers find LLM-synthesized Code World Models can achieve high prediction accuracy yet fail in gameplay due to pivotal dynamics omissions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers demonstrate that large language model-synthesized Code World Models (CWMs) can pass transition accuracy tests with near-perfect scores yet systematically lose in gameplay because critical rules are omitted. They identify a verified-versus-correct gap where less than 1% of errors cause significant play cost, and show this gap persists despite increased data or advanced models like GPT-5.x. The study also proves a quantitative law governing the harm from such omissions and extends the findings to imperfect-information games, suggesting that adequacy for planning-oriented world models should be evaluated based on search distribution or gameplay outcomes rather than sampled transition accuracy alone.

items.title: ReasFlow launches a knowledge-based multi-agent system for reasoning-centric scientific discovery in applied mathematics, autonomously generating research papers with rigorous proofs and synthesis [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: ReasFlow is an autonomous agent system designed to assist in theory-driven scientific discovery in applied mathematics by combining literature synthesis, algorithm design, theorem proving, experimentation, and manuscript preparation. It operates under a collaborative model where a human expert acts as Principal Investigator and the AI agent performs rigorous derivations, featuring an internal verification loop and automated knowledge retrieval to reduce expert intervention. The system has autonomously generated five complete research papers from minimal prompts, achieving top evaluation scores compared to state-of-the-art open-access baselines under a large language model-based review rubric. ReasFlow is publicly available on the ReasLab platform, offering a collaborative workspace for AI-assisted theoretical research.

items.title: Researchers introduce RxBrain, a foundation model combining language and visual reasoning for embodied cognition with joint planning and imagination [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: RxBrain is a new embodied cognition foundation model that integrates language and visual reasoning to represent embodied plans as single sequences combining task decomposition, planning, and world state prediction. It uses a unified multimodal Mixture-of-Transformers architecture trained on automatically generated text-visual planning supervision from embodied videos. The model supports joint understanding and generation of language, images, and videos, and shows promising results in continuous robot action generation without large-scale action-data pretraining, marking a step toward foundation models for embodied cognition.

items.title: Researchers analyze AI large language models' errors on conflict questions, revealing patterns of hallucination linked to thin data and rising generative engine optimization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers studied five leading AI large language model answer engines by asking 5,460 questions about 28 conflicts and comparing responses to documented evidence. They found that conflicts with sparse retrievable records led to more AI-generated errors such as invention, misattribution, and miscounting, exposing vulnerabilities to misinformation through generative engine optimization (GEO). Analysis of over 1,000 websites used by these AI models showed that GEO source optimization is already occurring, with state-partisan digital influence growing rapidly. The study highlights the challenges AI tools face in accurately representing conflict information, especially where data is limited, and argues for renewed emphasis on deep local monitoring and translation-based research that AI cannot replicate. The findings have implications for scholarship and policy amid the rise of GEO-driven information warfare, and the authors discuss future research directions in this evolving area.

items.title: Researchers propose shifting AI alignment from static preference emulation to dynamic, interactive human-AI workflows, highlighting new coordination challenges and a research agenda [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A new paper argues that current AI alignment methods, which rely on static models of human preferences, fail to capture the dynamic and context-dependent nature of real-world human-AI interactions. The authors propose a shift toward interactive and complementary alignment, where human and AI behaviors co-evolve over time, requiring a trajectory-level perspective rather than static emulation. The paper draws on insights from social science and interdisciplinary workshops to highlight how human-AI systems amplify coordination challenges and asymmetries in reasoning about uncertainty. It concludes by outlining a research agenda that calls for integrating machine learning with social and decision sciences to develop AI systems better aligned with humans through ongoing interaction.

items.title: Researchers find examples outperform prompts and guidance knobs in steering generative models by expanding property control beyond training data limits [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers show that generative models' ability to adjust properties using prompts or guidance scales hits a ceiling determined by the training data, which they call a "steering budget." They demonstrate that this budget splits into two parts: one reachable by traditional knobs and a larger part accessible only through providing concrete examples to the model. This approach allows models to move properties across their full range and target attributes that cannot be described in words. The team validates these findings with experiments in image and crystal-structure generation, offering a method to audit training data and construct example sets that fully utilize the steering budget.

items.title: Researchers propose automated multi-agent framework to synthesize hard adversarial examples for multimodal large language models, improving image safety benchmark robustness without human labeling [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce an automated agentic red-teaming system that generates challenging adversarial examples for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) used in content safety and moderation. The system uses a multi-agent architecture including a high-reasoning Architect agent, an advanced image generator, and a verification committee of LLM raters to autonomously identify policy edge cases and violations without human intervention. By incorporating these synthesized adversarial examples as in-context demonstrations during test-time retrieval, the approach significantly enhances model robustness, reducing the False Negative Rate from 41.2% to 24.5% on a public image safety benchmark. This method addresses the limitations of traditional active learning and manual annotation in scaling to complex multimodal threats.

items.title: Researchers validate context engineering as a key predictor of AI agent reliability using ProofAgent-Harness across seven criteria [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: A new study demonstrates that AI agents' failures are often due to weaknesses in their operating context rather than the agents themselves. Researchers developed ProofAgent-Harness, an open-source tool that evaluates context quality based on seven factors including role clarity, guardrail coverage, and instruction consistency, independently of agent behavior metrics. The study held large language model agents constant while varying their context, showing that specific context criteria predict corresponding behavioral outcomes such as hallucination resistance and manipulation resistance. These findings establish context measurement as a reliable preflight indicator for AI agent performance and suggest context engineering as an auditable layer for agent evaluation and governance.

items.title: Researchers develop and validate the Generative AI Reliance Types Scale to measure how undergraduates use AI in academic writing, based on a survey of 382 students at a U.S. Minority-Serving Institution [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: This study introduces the Generative AI Reliance Types Scale (GenAI-RTS), a 20-item instrument that categorizes student reliance on generative AI into four types: Strategic, Instrumental, Dependent, and Dialogic. Validation involved confirmatory factor analyses and interviews, confirming a five-factor structure with reliable subscales and measurement invariance across gender, first-generation status, and STEM majors. The scale differentiates students by AI literacy and writing outcomes, offering a validated tool for research and educational interventions related to AI use in academic writing.

items.title: Researchers analyze alignment between large language models' next-token distributions and empirical training data distributions, finding increased agreement with model scale but notable discrepancies [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: This paper examines how closely large language models' (LLMs) next-token output distributions match the empirical next-token distributions (ENTD) derived from their training data. The study finds that for many inputs, LLMs align almost perfectly with the ENTD, and this agreement improves with larger model scale and more training compute. However, there remains a significant subset of inputs where the model's predictions diverge from the empirical data distribution. The authors investigate potential causes for these discrepancies, including aspects of the transformer architecture, training procedures, and noise in estimating the ENTD. They propose "data-centric mechanistic interpretability" as a complementary approach to understanding how model behaviors emerge from training data rather than solely from learned weights.

items.title: Researchers propose Traccia, an OpenTelemetry-based AI governance platform that creates tamper-resistant compliance evidence aligned with EU AI Act requirements [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.content_text: The rapid advancement of large language models and AI-powered autonomous agents has exposed gaps in current software governance frameworks, particularly in meeting transparency and accountability standards like those in the EU AI Act. Researchers propose Traccia, a multi-level AI governance stack built on OpenTelemetry, designed to address these challenges by integrating telemetry data, semantic guardrail assessments, and execution lineage into a hashed trace ledger that generates tamper-resistant compliance evidence without compromising data privacy. Traccia aims to protect against threats such as alignment drift, SaaS security issues, and unauthorized deployment of shadow AI systems by providing a machine-readable foundation for enterprise-wide management of autonomous AI systems. The platform appends tamper-proof fingerprints and SHA-256 content hashes to compliance packages, mapping to specific regulatory articles, thereby bridging the gap between theoretical governance standards and practical implementation in AI system oversight.

items.title: Researchers present CIPHER, a decoupled exploration-selection framework that improves test-time scaling of data science AI agents by generating and selecting multiple initial states for concurrent execution [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: CIPHER is an automated data science agent designed to address the limitations of existing AI agents that rely on a single initial state, which can lead to cascading errors. By decoupling the generation of candidate initial states from their strategic selection, CIPHER enables concurrent execution of multiple states, enhancing robustness and performance across diverse data science tasks. The framework was evaluated on two benchmarks covering closed-form and open-form tasks, where it outperformed state-of-the-art methods using comparable models and remained competitive against larger language model baselines despite using a smaller base model. The study also analyzes how different generation and selection strategies, along with aggregator model capacity, impact overall performance, offering practical design recommendations for future AI agent development.

items.title: Researchers present Chat2Scenic, an iterative retrieval-augmented framework generating regulation-compliant autonomous driving scenario scripts with 76.42% compilation success rate [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce Chat2Scenic, a novel framework that uses iterative retrieval-augmented generation to create executable scenario scripts for autonomous driving validation, grounded in regulatory knowledge and domain-specific language syntax. The system supports interactive refinement via a chatbot interface and addresses limitations of previous methods by improving compilation success and framework accuracy. The team also proposes an open benchmark with 123 scenarios from regulations including NHTSA and United Nations Vehicle Regulations. Evaluations with state-of-the-art large language models show Chat2Scenic outperforms existing retrieval-assemble and full-script generation methods, achieving 76.42% compilation success rate and 58.17% framework accuracy compared to lower rates for prior approaches. The researchers have released their code as open source to support further research in this area.

items.title: Study compares machine learning models for short- and long-term forecasting of Egypt's EGX30 stock market, finding GRU and XGBoost most effective [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: This study evaluates various machine learning models to predict stock prices in Egypt's EGX30 market, focusing on both short- and long-term forecasts. Models assessed include K-Nearest Neighbours, random forest, extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), long short-term memory networks, and gated recurrent unit (GRU) networks, using historical EGX30 data and standard error metrics. The research aims to identify the most accurate models considering Egypt's unique market conditions to assist investors in decision-making. Results indicate that GRU outperforms other models for one-week to two-month forecasts, while XGBoost excels in one-day predictions. The study also highlights the value of ensemble techniques for long-term forecasts and notes the strong performance of K-Nearest Neighbours in long-term predictions, suggesting its continued relevance in financial technology applications.

items.title: Researchers introduce CatalogAgent, a Supervisor-mediated self-learning system that improves LLM-based generator and evaluator models for e-commerce catalog attribute prediction by over 13% [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: CatalogAgent is a novel system designed to enhance product catalog enrichment by addressing missing structured attribute values such as material, color, and shape. It uses a generator-evaluator framework based on large language models (LLMs), where a Supervisor Agent mediates conflicts between the generator and evaluator or external seller feedback to make final decisions. The system includes a Memory Base and Memory Summarizer that store and aggregate supervisory decisions to enable continuous self-improvement of the worker LLMs without human intervention. Through context engineering, CatalogAgent injects learnings from the Supervisor Agent into the generator and evaluator models, resulting in performance improvements of 15.24% and 13.98%, respectively. This approach demonstrates a new paradigm for self-learning generative AI systems that can improve accuracy in e-commerce catalog attribute prediction tasks.

items.title: Researchers test evaluation instruments for language-model honesty using a text-adventure game engine to measure verdict accuracy and propose a four-check integrity protocol [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers developed a text-adventure environment where the game engine, rather than the language model, determines quest completion status to evaluate the effects of different honesty assessment instruments. The language model must declare the quest complete, unreachable, or undecidable under a budget, with the engine scoring each verdict. The study found that changes in evaluation instruments significantly affected measured honesty, with verdict distributions varying across repeated runs and instrument configurations. The team preregistered decision rules and disclosed the strength of preregistration across series to ensure auditability. The experiment revealed that expanding verdict options and disclosing success criteria influenced the frequency of strong claims and false verdicts, while repeated runs showed non-stable verdict distributions. Two post-hoc patterns emerged: the presence of narrative register roughly doubled strong claims, and budget rendering affected verdicts more than register content. Despite compressing budgets toward scarcity landmarks, mediation tests returned null results. Based on these findings, the researchers propose a four-check integrity protocol to improve the reliability of language-model honesty evaluation instruments.

items.title: Researchers propose pairwise validator using frozen LLM to replace scalar rewards in self-evolving agents, matching full-reward baselines without labeled data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce a pairwise validator approach that uses a frozen large language model to compare parent and child agent versions, providing binary judgments instead of scalar rewards in self-evolving agent loops. This method reduces the need for costly labeled data and domain expertise typically required for reward design. The validator was integrated into three existing self-evolving engines and tested on prompt and code artifacts, achieving comparable or better task accuracy than traditional reward-based methods. The approach offers a drop-in replacement for reward signals, simplifying agent evolution without sacrificing performance.

items.title: Researchers introduce CausalGraphX, a counterfactual graph neural network framework for explainable systemic risk assessment in financial networks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: CausalGraphX is a new framework that combines graph neural networks with counterfactual reasoning to assess systemic risk in interconnected financial systems. It uses graph attention mechanisms and adversarial regularization to capture causal drivers of institutional vulnerability and generates counterfactual explanations for stress testing and intervention planning. The framework was validated on large-scale synthetic financial networks, outperforming traditional and deep learning models in predicting cascading defaults while providing actionable and interpretable insights.

items.title: Researchers find per-token fixed-point convergence in depth-recurrent transformers with variable inference depths on a 135M-parameter model [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A study on a 135M-parameter depth-recurrent transformer trained on FineWeb-Edu shows that the model's recurrent state converges to a fixed point per token, with convergence speed varying by token type. The median token stabilizes by the sixth loop, while about 10% of tokens continue updating at the training-mean depth of eight, with whitespace tokens converging fastest and content words slowest. The researchers demonstrate that a training-free rule halting token updates upon output stabilization reduces average inference depth by 38% without loss in quality, outperforming a learned linear router. The experiments ran on a single RTX 4090 GPU over approximately 100 hours, and the study reports average depth as a proxy for computational cost without claiming realized speedup or FLOP parity.

items.title: Researchers release Tactile, an open-source tool layer that improves software agents' interaction with desktop applications by converting UI evidence into verifiable, semantic actions [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers have developed Tactile, an open-source tool layer designed to enhance software agents' ability to interact with desktop applications more reliably. Unlike traditional methods that rely on predicting screen coordinates from screenshots, Tactile integrates operating system accessibility semantics, OCR-grounded text, and visual fallback regions to create action-grounded interface states that support observation, grounding, action, and verification loops. Testing on macOSWorld-style tasks showed that Tactile improved Codex's success rate from 41.1% to 50.0% overall and from 45.2% to 55.3% on accessibility-adapted tasks, with consistent gains across multiple agents including Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, and Goose. These results indicate that reliable computer use by agents requires not only stronger models but also a reusable execution substrate that exposes software actions as semantic, verifiable, and auditable objects rather than anonymous screen coordinates.

items.title: Researchers introduce Step-Level Preference Learning to improve generative agents in social simulations using 57K human annotations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers developed an interactive simulation interface called Step-Level Preference Learning to collect fine-grained human preference annotations on intermediate decision steps of large language model-based generative agents. This dataset of 57,000 annotations enables supervised finetuning and direct preference optimization on open-weight language models, enhancing simulation fidelity, coordination, interaction quality, and socially effective agent behavior. Their results demonstrate that step-level human supervision effectively improves both local decision-making and long-horizon agent behavior in social simulations.

items.title: SAGA introduces schema-aware grounding to improve agentic text-to-SPARQL generation, achieving top F1 and exact-match accuracy on Wikidata and Freebase benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: SAGA is a training-free framework designed to enhance semantic parsing for complex knowledge base question answering by incorporating schema constraints into property exploration. It maintains a bidirectional type state and filters incompatible property candidates to reduce semantically invalid queries that yield empty results. Evaluated across nine benchmark settings on Wikidata and Freebase, SAGA outperforms existing methods by achieving the highest F1 scores on all benchmarks and the highest exact-match accuracy on eight, while also reducing empty-result queries on Wikidata.

items.title: Researchers propose CEDI framework for dynamic, multi-turn evaluation of vision language models, revealing more realistic visual hallucinations than static tests [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce CEDI (Contextualized Evaluations of MLLMs through Dynamic, multi-round Interactions), a framework that evaluates multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) through interactive, multi-turn conversations involving an evaluatee model, an automated examiner, and a grader. This approach addresses the gap between static benchmark tests and real-world applications by using graph-based task representations and diverse probing strategies to assess model performance, particularly focusing on visual hallucinations. Applying CEDI across multiple models, datasets, and domains, the study finds that interactive evaluations detect significantly more hallucinations that better reflect practical use cases compared to conventional static evaluations. The research also shows that hallucinations tend to accumulate over extended dialogue contexts and that models are especially vulnerable to questions requiring premise rejection or refusal, highlighting the need for more ecologically valid assessments of MLLM capabilities.

items.title: Researchers propose VLT, a multimodal foundation model integrating time-series, frequency-spectrum visuals, and text for industrial equipment prognostics [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce VLT, a multimodal foundation model designed to improve Prognostics and Health Management (PHM) for industrial equipment by jointly modeling time-series data, frequency-spectrum visual representations, and textual knowledge. The model uses the frequency spectrum as a visual bridge to connect continuous temporal signals with discrete semantics, addressing limitations of single-modality approaches in complex industrial scenarios. VLT incorporates a Time-aware Mixture-of-Experts to capture diverse temporal dynamics and a Frequency-Text Augmented Learner for joint spectral and semantic feature modeling within a shared space. A time-centric gradient alignment mechanism mitigates cross-modal optimization conflicts. Experiments on multiple industrial datasets show that VLT outperforms state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating enhanced robustness and generalization under few-shot, noisy, and incomplete-modality conditions.

items.title: RetroAgent uses large language models with structured memory to improve multi-step retrosynthesis planning, enhancing exploration and decision-making in chemical synthesis [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: RetroAgent is a new approach that combines large language models with structured memory to tackle multi-step retrosynthesis planning, which involves breaking down target molecules into commercially available building blocks through feasible reaction sequences. This method allows the agent to consider the full search state, including explored routes and intermediate properties, enabling more informed decisions than traditional methods that score candidates in isolation. The system bridges symbolic search and neural reasoning by integrating memory and chemistry tools, allowing it to observe global progress and domain knowledge simultaneously. Experiments on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution benchmarks show that RetroAgent achieves strong performance and generalization in retrosynthesis tasks.

items.title: WrAFT launches modular automated writing evaluation system for argumentative essays using LLMs, achieving state-of-the-art scoring accuracy and high human approval for feedback [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: WrAFT is a new Writing Assessment and Feedback Tool designed to provide accurate scores and comprehensive feedback for argumentative essays. It uses a modular approach dividing tasks into scoring, surface-level feedback, and deep-level feedback, leveraging large language models like LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct, GPT-4o, and Claude 3.7. The system was trained and evaluated on a proprietary dataset of 480 TOEFL Independent Writing essays with official benchmark scores, achieving a quadratic weighted kappa of 0.84 and root mean square error of 0.44 on a 0-5 scale. Human evaluations show high approval ratings for the feedback generated by WrAFT, with 96.14% for surface-level, 93.03% for deep-level macro, and 94.69% for deep-level micro feedback. An interactive user interface for the system has been developed and is publicly available for free use.

items.title: Researchers present Atrex-Bench, a production-trace-driven GPU kernel benchmark, and Atrex-Kernel-Agent, an optimization tool that improves LLM-generated kernels to match or exceed hand-tuned baselines [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce Atrex-Bench, a GPU kernel benchmark based on 30 operators and 440 shapes sampled from real production inference traces on compute-limited, memory-rich GPUs, weighted by observed GPU time to emphasize impactful kernels. Evaluations of six leading coding agents show that even the best models achieve only about 10% of the hardware roofline, with correctness metrics overstating capability due to reliance on PyTorch fallbacks rather than generated kernels. To address this gap, the team co-released Atrex-Kernel-Agent (AKA), a profile-driven kernel optimization agent that uses iterative measure-revise search, optimization dropout to escape stalled searches, and a layered knowledge base of reference kernels and optimization documents. In controlled tests, AKA successfully converts fallback kernels into optimized kernels that meet or surpass hand-tuned production baselines, demonstrating progress toward production-ready LLM-generated GPU kernels.

items.title: Researchers propose Intention Abstraction Layer middleware to detect and explain goal conflicts among autonomous industrial subsystems before execution [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Modern industrial environments operate multiple autonomous subsystems simultaneously, each with distinct goals but sharing physical resources, leading to conflicts that are often detected only after failures. Researchers propose the Intention Abstraction Layer (IAL), a domain-agnostic middleware that represents intentions as persistent, explainable runtime objects, using a large language model grounded in an OWL ontology to parse natural language goals into structured intentions. The IAL includes a consistency monitor that detects conflicts at registration time and a transparency module that explains conflicts in natural language, shifting assurance from post-failure analysis to pre-execution checking. A proof of concept demonstrated the IAL detecting and explaining conflicting production and energy intentions registered by two autonomous agents before execution, preventing potential operational issues. This approach aims to improve cooperation among autonomous systems by ensuring alignment with high-level human intentions and avoiding unintended conflicts in industrial settings.

items.title: Researchers propose Seer framework to accelerate Diffusion Multimodal Large Language Models by detecting semantic boundaries via MLP activation sparsity and truncating redundant output tokens [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Diffusion Multimodal Large Language Models (DMLLMs) face efficiency challenges due to fixed-length output padding that causes redundant computation. Researchers introduce Seer, a training-free method that identifies the valid semantic boundary at the first denoising step using a Signal-to-Noise Ratio criterion and truncates unnecessary output tokens to improve inference speed. Seer employs a hybrid execution strategy to maintain throughput during batched serving while accommodating dynamic sequence lengths. Experiments across nine benchmarks show Seer can accelerate throughput by up to 31 times without degrading performance and even slightly improves accuracy on complex visual tasks by reducing noise leakage, offering a plug-and-play solution for DMLLM acceleration.

items.title: Researchers introduce Information Flow Graph monitor to detect and block covert security regressions in AI agent deployments, improving infrastructure safety [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: AI software development agents can modify critical infrastructure and security systems, sometimes completing tasks while covertly weakening safeguards. Researchers propose an Information Flow Graph (IFG) monitor that analyzes structural security regressions using control-flow and data-flow graph differences alongside code diffs to detect such sabotage in infrastructure-as-code settings. The IFG monitor outperforms untrained git diff monitors by reducing missed attacks from 11.6% to 3.5% at a 1% false positive rate and can operate synchronously to block suspicious changes before deployment. In synchronous mode, IFG real-time rollback eliminated covert task success without affecting legitimate task completion, suggesting untrained structural monitors offer a practical approach to safer AI agent deployment for organizations lacking complex monitoring resources.

items.title: Researchers introduce Alipay-PIBench, a benchmark for evaluating coding agents on realistic Alipay payment integration with nine projects and 18 tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Alipay-PIBench is a new benchmark designed to assess coding agents' ability to handle realistic payment integration tasks involving Alipay. It includes nine product-specific projects and 18 task instances, divided into basic functional completion and advanced risk-aware scenarios, with evaluation supported by deterministic checks and large language model-assisted semantic assessments. Six coding-agent models were tested, showing that access to specialized payment integration skills improved performance by over 10 percentage points on average. The benchmark offers a controlled environment to diagnose model capabilities and evaluate structured guidance in payment integration tasks.

items.title: Researchers study network-efficiency effects in groups of 16 large language model agents performing the Mason-Watts spatial search task, comparing their performance with Bayesian optimization agents and human data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers investigated how network topology affects collective problem solving in groups of large language model (LLM) agents using the Mason-Watts experiment, which involves a two-dimensional search task. They tested sixteen LLM agents across eight network topologies and compared their results with mechanistic Bayesian optimization agents and human experimental data. The study found that LLM agents showed significant network-efficiency effects only when given a one-sentence instruction to randomize their first-round choices, which improved collective payoff substantially compared to default initialization. The Bayesian optimization agents outperformed the LLM agents on this spatial search task. The researchers also analyzed differences in exploration-exploitation behavior, copying, and spatial diversity among the agents, providing insights into how communication network structure influences collaborative learning and problem solving in AI agent groups.

items.title: Multi-LLM Collaborative MRI Report Generation for Visual Instruction Tuning in Brain Oncology [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2607.14581v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and their extension to vision-language models (VLMs) have made it easier to combine text and images for tasks such as report generation. Existing VLMs in medicine typically focus on 2D images (chest X-rays), and their extension to 3D imaging has been difficult because of the lack of paired 3D imaging-text data. Thus, we introduce a new method for creating a 3D image-text dataset for brain oncology using 3D MRI scans of glioma and meningioma cases. We use a cooperative system in which several LLMs work together to generate and check reports, ensuring that they are accurate and clear. By leveraging the new 3D MRI-text dataset, we further build a VLM that converts MRI scans into tokens and aligns them with text instructions. Our VLM performed better in report generation and visual question answering tasks than other 2D and 3D methods. Our method not only improves the quality of reports but also helps with better diagnosis and treatment in brain oncology.

items.title: MathCoPilot: An Interactive System for Human-AI Symbiotic Paradigm of Mathematical Research [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2607.14582v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing LLM-based theorem provers have achieved impressive results on formal mathematics benchmarks, yet they remain confined to acting as autonomous agents that prove a stated proposition. In this paper, we propose MathCoPilot, a human-in-the-loop system that embodies a new human--AI symbiotic paradigm for mathematical research, in which the mathematician steers the high-level mathematical direction while AI agents carry out the detailed formalization and proof work under continuous human guidance. MathCoPilot unifies three core capabilities: (1) an interactive workbench where the mathematician and AI agents collaborate through a living proof blueprint that decomposes a proof into navigable steps the human can directly inspect, direct, and refine; (2) automated proving skill orchestration with adaptive knowledge base search and Lean-integrated iterative verification; and (3) topic-driven paper retrieval and automated formalization into a verified Lean knowledge base. Using MathCoPilot, we systematically compare four state-of-the-art LLMs, including Gemini~3.1~Pro, GPT-5.4, and Claude~Opus~4.7, on a FormalMATH subset and on two real PDE theorems requiring deep domain expertise, evaluating their ability to produce verified Lean~4 proofs and to identify errors in deliberately incorrect proofs. Our results show that while current models can handle undergraduate-level problems with high success rates under favorable autoformalization conditions, substantial challenges remain for domain-specific theorems requiring genuine mathematical understanding.

items.title: SportD: Can VLMs Physically Strategize? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2607.14616v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision--language models have become increasingly capable of interpreting visual scenes, but it remains unclear whether they can use information to make strategically effective decisions. We investigate this question in soccer, where models observe the seconds preceding an on-ball decision and must choose whether to shoot or pass to a specific teammate. Unlike conventional visual-understanding tasks, soccer enables decisions to be evaluated quantitatively by estimating the value of every available action. We introduce SportD, a benchmark comprising 478 on-ball decisions from the 2022 FIFA World Cup. Each model choice is evaluated against a possession-value model that estimates the action that most increases the attacking team's probability of scoring, allowing us to measure both optimal-action accuracy and the value forfeited by suboptimal decisions. Across three frontier VLMs, the best selects the highest-valued action on 31.4% of events, compared with 38.9% for the professional players, and all models incur significantly greater regret. Further analysis reveals a systematic preference for lower-variance and lower-reward actions: VLMs shoot less often and select substantially less progressive passes than either the optimal policy or the real players. The models also reproduce the player's specific action above chance even when that action is suboptimal, suggesting partial imitation of familiar play patterns rather than consistent evaluation of counterfactual alternatives. SportD provides a value-grounded testbed for measuring physical strategic reasoning in VLMs.

items.title: Action QFormer: Structured Representation Shaping under Action Supervision in Vision-Language-Action Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2607.14635v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Action supervision in vision-language-action (VLA) models is often treated as a downstream objective for learning action prediction. In this paper, we study it instead as a force that shapes inherited multimodal representations. We show that this shaping has a dual effect: it is necessary for forming action-compatible representations, but when action supervision is applied too directly to the inherited multimodal pathway, it can also destabilize representations that support language-side processing and object grounding. To address this tension, we introduce Action QFormer, a query-based action-facing interface that uses instruction-conditioned queries to reorganize inherited multimodal information into action-facing representations before downstream action generation. In zero-shot sim-to-real navigation, Action QFormer improves average closed-loop task success from 18.8% to 56.3%, raises fixed-instruction action-generation correctness from 22.5% to 75.5%, and nearly eliminates out-of-distribution instruction generations. Further analyses show that Action QFormer changes how action supervision shapes inherited multimodal representations, reducing broad upstream rewriting while preserving targeted and sometimes constructive action-supervised adaptation. These results suggest that improving VLA performance requires not only stronger pretrained backbones, but also better ways of selecting and organizing inherited multimodal information while controlling how it is shaped under action supervision.

items.title: Analytic Abduction: Causal Decomposition and Governed Commitment for Human--AI Coordination [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2607.14641v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Abductive reasoning operates in two directions. The synthetic mode builds explanations from available hypotheses; the analytic mode, conversely, identifies the latent factors whose interaction accounts for a complex observed state. This paper develops the analytic mode as a non-greedy, risk-sensitive discipline of commitment, in which candidate factors coexist and interact, resolving into committed conclusions only when explicit governance conditions are met. The formal core is the $\kappa$-$\tau$ apparatus: $\kappa$ encodes the epistemic interaction among hypotheses, and $\tau$ sets a commitment threshold calibrated to the decision's stakes. The central contribution is the causal cluster, a structured object recording which latent factors participate in a decomposition, with what weights and interaction structure, together with a two-level architecture (intra-cluster $\kappa^*$, inter-cluster $\kappa^{**}$) that guards against causal misattribution. Demonstrated in epidemiological crisis decomposition and adversarial cyber threat analysis, the framework's contribution to human-AI reasoning is the legibility of suspended decomposition as a shared coordination object, providing structural resistance to premature convergence. In practice, the decision-maker is handed not a single imposed answer but the competing explanatory scenarios, weighted by plausibility and paired with the evidence that would resolve between them, so that sound action is possible even before the ambiguity is resolved.

items.title: MCPEvol-Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agent Performance Across Dynamic Evolutions of MCP Servers [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2607.14642v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers emerge as the core infrastructure for connecting LLMs with external tools, existing benchmarks leverage real-world MCP servers to evaluate LLM agents' tool-using capabilities. However, these benchmarks overlook the continuous evolution of tool interfaces and functionalities within MCP servers, resulting in flawed assessments that fail to capture the agent's adaptability in changing tool landscapes. To bridge this gap, we introduce \textbf{MCPEvol-Bench}, a novel benchmark for evaluating the task-solving capabilities of LLM agents under dynamic toolset evolution. Inspired by large-scale empirical study, we propose 11 mutation operators to simulate realistic tool evolution within 123 MCP servers. We benchmark 12 state-of-the-art LLMs on multiple versions of MCP servers, revealing that even frontier models struggle to adapt to evolving tools. For instance, GPT-5.4 and Claude-Sonnet-4-6 exhibit performance declines of 13.7\% and 14.4\% in evolved MCP servers, respectively, accompanied by substantial increases in planning and reasoning errors. These findings highlight the vulnerability of LLM-driven workflows, establishing MCPEvol-Bench as a standard for evaluating agent adaptability in dynamic tool environments.

items.title: TopoAgent: A Self-Evolving Topological Agent for Multimodal Scientific Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2607.14658v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) excel in general tasks, rigorous scientific reasoning remains challenging due to the limitations of monolithic, linear planning. Such sequential designs often suffer from visual-semantic misalignment, long-context hallucinations, and brittle execution under fixed task granularity. We propose TopoAgent, a self-evolving topological framework that replaces linear trajectories with dynamic, state-isolated graph evolution. TopoAgent first employs a front-end decomposer to fracture complex queries into visually-grounded atoms. These atoms are organized into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) based on their dependencies, enabling strict context isolation to shield the reasoning engine from irrelevant historical noise. Furthermore, we introduce adaptive atomic fission, which dynamically splits bottleneck nodes into finer-grained sub-atoms at runtime when tool capability boundaries are exceeded. Extensive experiments across mathematics, physics, and chemistry benchmarks demonstrate that TopoAgent significantly outperforms state-of-the-art linear agent frameworks, providing a robust, noise-resistant, and self-correcting paradigm for autonomous scientific reasoning.

items.title: SmartRAG: Native Graph-Based RAG for Mobile Device [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2607.14661v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deploying large language models (LLMs) as personal assistants on mobile devices demands privacy, low latency, and offline availability, yet the computational cost of giant models clashes with strict edge-hardware budgets. We argue that this tension cannot be resolved by model compression alone; it requires decomposing on-device intelligence into complementary functional roles. We present SmartRAG, a fully on-device framework that organizes an intelligent assistant around four coordinated modules -- Perception, Memory, Focus, and Thinking. At the core of SmartRAG is EvoNER, a continually learnable named-entity recognizer that incrementally expands its label inventory through teacher-distilled updates, enabling the system to absorb previously unseen entity types without retraining the backbone LLM. Extracted knowledge is stored in MRGraph, a three-layer provenance-preserving knowledge graph, and retrieved at query time through a hybrid pipeline combining graph traversal, lexical matching, and dense semantic search. The on-device LLM is invoked only for high-value semantic operations -- labeling, planning, and answer synthesis -- keeping inference costs bounded. Experiments on four QA benchmarks (TriviaQA, Natural Questions, HotpotQA, MultiHopQA) show that SmartRAG with a quantized 1.7B-parameter backbone achieves multi-hop reasoning performance competitive with models up to 18$\times$ larger, while running entirely on commodity smartphones within practical memory and latency envelopes.

items.title: Project Kaleidoscope: Contextual, Human-Aligned Evaluation for Real-World AI Applications [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2607.14673v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evaluations (Evals) are a deployment bottleneck for real-world AI applications: public benchmarks rarely match a team's users, context, or policies, and human review is often tedious to scale. Motivated by our work with AI applications in the public sector, this project addresses recurring evaluation challenges encountered when applications must satisfy local policy and governance requirements. We present Kaleidoscope, an integrated workflow for contextual functional evaluation that links persona-based test generation, contextualized rubrics, and human review for reliability-gated automated scoring. Generated test cases are scored against application-specific rubrics; human annotations provide reviewable labels; and LLM judges automate scoring only when their agreement with those labels meets a configured threshold. Kaleidoscope is therefore a practical, inspectable, iterative workflow for product teams. We report early evidence from a three-week pilot across four organizational use cases and custom-rubric judge experiments on 108 annotated Q\&A pairs spanning four domains and 14 evaluation dimensions. The results highlight useful features for end-to-end reliable, automated scoring.

items.title: Stop Thinking, Start Looking: Efficient Post-Training for Multimodal Document Question Answering via Reasoning-Free Alignment [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2607.14682v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Efficient multimodal document question answering with explicit visual grounding, locating the precise document region that supports each answer remains an open challenge. Current approaches bifurcate into Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), which requires large annotated datasets and reaches optimization plateaus, and reasoning-centric Reinforcement Learning (RL), which depends on verbose intermediate traces that inflate inference token cost without clear benefit. We introduce Perception-RFT, a training framework that applies Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to multimodal document QA, bypassing intermediate reasoning tokens to directly align visual features with structured grounding outputs. To rigorously evaluate the necessity of reasoning, we construct a reasoning variant under identical reward settings. We find that reasoning-enabled models suppress their reasoning traces during training, converging to direct perception-based policies at the 4B parameter scale, reducing per-query inference token length by more than 60%, while reasoning-enabled RL underperforms perception-only training. Through a fine-grained analysis of Qwen3-VL-4B optimization dynamics, we confirm that SFT saturation and cold-start RL instability established in text-domain post-training extend to multimodal, and identify a previously uncharacterized Grounding Divergence: a selective trade-off between semantic robustness and geometric precision on two out of distribution (OOD) benchmarks (4,828 samples) under joint RL optimization. We further show that an early SFT$\rightarrow$RL transition achieves comparable precision with 65% less training data.

items.title: InCarEmo: A Multimodal Dataset for In-Cabin Emotion Recognition and Driver State Monitoring [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2607.14683v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding driver emotion and state is critical for the next generation of intelligent in-cabin systems that ensure safety and enhance human-vehicle interaction. However, existing public datasets for in-cabin affective computing are largely limited to visual modalities and rarely include conversational information, making it difficult to capture the linguistic and interactive cues underlying driver emotion. To address these gaps, we introduce InCarEmo, a multimodal dataset for in-cabin emotion recognition and driver state monitoring. InCarEmo integrates RGB and infrared video, in-cabin audio, and dialogue text collected from scripted in-cabin scenarios designed to simulate realistic driver behaviors, covering diverse lighting conditions and driving contexts. The dataset supports three primary tasks: 1) multimodal emotion recognition, 2) fatigue detection, and 3) distraction monitoring. In addition to the original Chinese data, we construct an auxiliary English benchmark to support preliminary cross-lingual evaluation. We provide a unified benchmark with extensive baseline results across unimodal and multimodal methods, including analyses under modality-missing and noise conditions. Experimental results demonstrate the benefits of multimodal fusion and reveal remaining challenges under real-world noise and low-light conditions. By releasing InCarEmo, we aim to establish a comprehensive foundation for robust, interpretable, and human-centric in-cabin affective understanding, promoting safer and more empathetic driver-vehicle interaction.

items.title: AI vs Human Expert Reasoning: Assessing Agreements in Building Typology Predictions based on Street View Imagery [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2607.14756v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This research investigates the potential of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to infer building typologies: Construction, Current Use, and Storeys from Google Street View (GSV) images. Predictions generated by VLMs are compared with inference by human experts (civil engineers and architects) as a source of manually labelled ground-truth data. We evaluate several state-of-the-art VLMs, including GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Gemini 2.0 Flash. By applying different scaling strategies and prompting techniques, we found that Chain-of-Thought prompts provide an overall more stable model performance. We also investigate the reasoning behind VLMs' building-typology predictions by examining the probabilities of keywords appearing in AI explanations. This enabled us to analyse patterns in these reasonings and identify key themes driving both agreements and disagreements between VLM and expert labels. We find that AI tends to focus on visual indicators, whereas human experts place greater emphasis on broader contextual cues and domain knowledge, in addition to visual cues. Overall, VLM can approximate experts' capability in building-typology classification at scale, with an average accuracy of approximately 70%. The study demonstrates the VLM's potential for AI automation in tasks that require pattern recognition and object identification in an urban context. AI have the potential to serve as complementary and collaborative tools for urban analysis, leveraging their strengths in understanding visual patterns. This study contributes to the exploration of the efficiency and scalability of AI visual prediction and provides insights into the reasoning processes that could support automation processes in urban analysis and prediction.

items.title: Global Index on Responsible AI: 2026 Report [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2607.14782v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Grounded in human rights-based frameworks such as the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, the Global Index on Responsible AI (GIRAI) examines how countries translate responsible AI commitments into enforceable protections, institutional capacity, and redress mechanisms. GIRAI 2026 assesses these across five dimensions: Inclusion and Diversity, Ethics and Sustainability, Labour and Skills, Trust and Safety, and AI Use in Public Service. A global network of 135 country-level researchers collected and assessed 68,138 data points on 38 indicators organised across three pillars: government AI policy and implementation (17 indicators), civil society engagement (5), enabling conditions (15), and documented cases of government deployment of unacceptable-risk AI systems. The data covers November 2023 to September 2025. A score of 100 is derived from the indicators to rank all countries. Findings show that while responsible AI governance is expanding, with 126 of 135 countries having at least one government policy or initiative across the 17 AI Policy indicators, this does not often translate into meaningful protection. For instance, Global South countries account for 203 of 306 new cases of indicators with frameworks since the first edition, yet 78% of their frameworks remain non-binding compared with 42% in the Global North. Government commitment to AI governance also does not extend to their own algorithms: whereas Transparency and Explainability is the strongest performing indicator, with 58% of countries having some framework, only 18% require Public Disclosure of Government Algorithms. Credible evidence of government deployment of unacceptable-risk AI systems was also found in 35 countries. These findings show that responsible AI governance must move beyond framework adoption toward enforceable rights-based protections, resourced oversight institutions, and accessible redress.

items.title: Transcoders for Investigating Deception in Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2607.14791v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transcoders have recently emerged as a promising approach for mechanistic interpretability (MI), enabling circuit-level analysis of model behaviour. In this paper, we investigate the use of transcoders to analyse deceptive behaviour in language models, a behaviour that poses a safety and security risk. Using a Qwen3-4B model with pre-trained transcoders, specifically per-layer transcoders (PLTs), we construct attribution graphs that capture feature activations and inter-feature dependencies, allowing circuit-level analysis of deception. Through feature steering and circuit analysis, we identified a dictionary of deception-related features and show that these features exert a stronger influence on deceptive outputs, as they produce predictable shifts between deceptive and non-deceptive responses. These findings suggest that deception emerges from internal model mechanisms and highlight the potential of transcoders for behavioural monitoring and early detection of security vulnerabilities related to malicious behaviours in language models.

items.title: CrimeNER Demo: Named-Entity Recognition in the Crime Domain [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2607.14800v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present CrimeNER Demo, an AI-powered platform that enables us to extract general crime-related information from documents and classify them into entity types with two levels of granularity. We provide pretrained NER models on the CrimeNER database, and we give the possibility to users to provide their own annotated data to train models for their own specific cases. This demonstrator aims to promote crime-related NER research and provides a practical tool to automatically extract crime information for researchers and law enforcement agencies. The demonstrator includes: i) Pretrained NER models on the crime domain; ii) Possibility to finetune the models on specific data annotated by the user; and iii) An automatic pipeline to extract and annotate crime entities from documents. The demo platform, a tutorial to run the demo, and a video demonstration are publicly available on GitHub.

items.title: Reachability-Aware Pretraining for Efficient Target-Oriented Path Exploration in Temporal Knowledge Graph Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2607.14886v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Temporal Knowledge Graph (TKG) reasoning under the extrapolation setting focuses on forecasting future time-stamped events (facts) from historical data in a temporal knowledge graph. Existing approaches, reinforcement learning (RL)-based multi-hop reasoning methods are prominent for TKG reasoning because they produce human-interpretable predictions via explicit multi-hop path tracing. However, during RL training, rewards are typically sparse, and exploration is highly inefficient due to the vast, time-evolving action space. These issues hinder efficient training and often limit overall performance. To address these challenges, we propose RAPTOR (Reachability-Aware Pretraining for Efficient Target-Oriented Path Exploration), a self-supervised pretraining method that injects a reachability-aware inductive bias to the agent. By learning to estimate the reachability of candidate actions to the target entity, RAPTOR reduces exploration over unpromising paths and provides a strong initialization for downstream RL fine-tuning. Experimental results on the ICEWS14, ICEWS05-15, and ICEWS18 datasets demonstrate that RAPTOR pretraining markedly improves the training efficiency and consistently outperforms conventional baselines, establishing it as an effective approach for enhancing RL-based multi-hop reasoning methods for TKG reasoning.

items.title: Proof-or-Stop: Don't Trust the Agent, Trust the Evidence -- Loop Engineering for Verifiable Evidence-Gated Lifecycle Control [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2607.14890v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous coding agents increasingly execute multi-step software work, but lifecycle states such as reviewed, tested, DONE, and ready-to-merge remain claims unless supported by current evidence. We present Proof-or-Stop Lifecycle Control, a method that permits lifecycle transitions only when fresh, tracked-source-state-bound, mechanically verifiable evidence satisfies the relevant gate. The method treats agent outputs as claims rather than lifecycle state, and uses proof operationally to mean gate-admissible evidence under a stated trust model, not semantic program correctness. We evaluate an open-source implementation through mechanism tests, a powered control-policy ablation, and operated self-application evidence. The unattended-loop engine passed 10 of 10 scenarios with zero false-DONE, and local-key receipt bundles rejected 18 tamper classes with zero false accepts. In a 9,240-cell ablation, the pre-registered A4 versus A2-prime comparison reduced visible-pass/hidden-fail amplification from 31 of 1,800 injected cells under a compute-budgeted naive loop to 2 of 1,800 under the gated loop, a 1.6 percentage-point improvement in not-amplified rate with a 95 percent confidence interval of [0.8, 2.5]. A near-compute A3 versus A4 comparison, 14 of 1,800 versus 2 of 1,800, indicates that the gain is associated with enforcing review as a lifecycle gate rather than merely adding a reviewer. The self-application corpus contains 565 stories and 1,007 review findings, with 94.8 percent resolved, plus a 68-row high/critical cross-vendor exhibit. These results support Proof-or-Stop as a model-agnostic, host-neutral control layer for deciding which autonomous-agent claims a lifecycle may act on. The evaluation is limited to one model family, 24 ablation tasks, and a self-hosted corpus.

items.title: Contextualized Early Detection of Online Firestorms: A Sequential LLM-Based Approach [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2607.14957v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Online firestorms are rapid collective escalations of highly negative user-generated content and may cause substantial reputational and economic damage. Existing detectors usually work with volume signals, sentiment scores, or predefined linguistic features.
